solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Appearance in county's principal city

indicators.note: in says one piece sits inside the abbreviation for county

parts.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for county
an air is a manner or appearance, as in 'an air of confidence'

explanation.surface: Someone notices a figure showing up in the main town of a county.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital of Egypt, so it is that country's principal city.

clue.text: Polite figures from Ancient Rome

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for 100
IV is the Roman numeral for 4
I is the Roman numeral for 1
L is the Roman numeral for 50

explanation.surface: Courteous characters from classical Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figures' looks like people but means numerals: C, IV, I, L.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe courteous, well-mannered behaviour.

clue.text: Being out to lunch isn't any stranger after one

indicators.note: after places the shuffled letters behind the numeral for one

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: stranger says the letters are made odder, rearranged

explanation.surface: Taking a lunch break is no odder than anything else once one o'clock has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out to lunch' is slang for crazy, not on a meal break.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out to lunch is slang for being mad, so the state of madness fits.

clue.text: A bad actor with Oscar from South American city

indicators.note: from South means, in a down answer, the letters are read upwards from the bottom

parts.note: a ham is an over-acting performer
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A poor performer, Oscar winner in hand, hails from a South American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' looks like one phrase, but 'from South' is the reversal signal and 'American city' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in Nebraska, in the United States.

clue.text: Unstylish prop, dreadfully hard to find?

indicators.note: dreadfully says the words are mangled into a different order

explanation.surface: A theatre prop so unfashionable that nobody can lay hands on one.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for scarce, with too little available to meet demand.

clue.text: Vain person in a heap after PE

indicators.note: after places the article and the heap behind the letters of PE

parts.note: a cock is a conical heap of hay, as in haycock

explanation.surface: A conceited pupil collapses in a pile after gym class.
explanation.walkthrough: PE (physical education, school gym lessons) is used as its own letters. A cock, or haycock, is a small pile of hay.
explanation.definitionFit: The showy bird is a byword for vanity, so a strutting, vain person is called one.

clue.text: Soon member of clergy's heading off

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter is removed

parts.note: a canon is a member of the clergy attached to a cathedral

explanation.surface: A cleric will be setting off shortly.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic word meaning shortly or presently, as in 'I'll see you by and by'.

clue.text: Carol, crossing Scottish river, is going nowhere

indicators.note: crossing says the word for carol spans the river, holding it inside

parts.note: to carol is to sing
the Tay is Scotland's longest river

explanation.surface: A carol singer wading a Scottish river gets stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carol' looks like a name but is the verb meaning to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: Remaining in one place means not leaving, so not moving on.

clue.text: Fanatic going after primate's bit of food

indicators.note: going after places the word for fanatic behind the primate in the answer

parts.note: a monkey is a primate
a nut is an enthusiast or fanatic, as in 'a golf nut'

explanation.surface: A zealot chases an ape's snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Another name for the peanut, a small edible item often sold as a snack.

clue.text: Panorama is a TV broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast in its old sense of scattered widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Panorama, the BBC current-affairs show, is a television broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is the long-running BBC documentary programme, which makes 'TV broadcast' look like plain description.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean a wide, sweeping view of scenery.

clue.text: Journalist with Japanese money returned in carriage

parts.note: a hack is a journalist, often a jobbing one

indicators.note: returned means the currency word is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: the yen is the currency of Japan

explanation.surface: A reporter gets his yen sent back while riding in a coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A hackney is a horse-drawn vehicle for hire, the ancestor of the hackney cab.

clue.text: Silver ring found on pine in the distant past

indicators.note: found on means the silver and ring are attached next to the word for pine

parts.note: to pine for something is to long for it
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A silver ring turns up on a pine tree, or in a pine box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pine' looks like the tree but is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for a time far back, many years previously.

clue.text: Motorist association swindle taking in old forest dweller

parts.note: the RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation

indicators.note: taking in means the swindle word holds the abbreviation for old inside it

parts.note: a con is a swindle

explanation.surface: A motoring club falls for a scam involving an elderly woodland resident.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British breakdown and motoring organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: A masked North American mammal that lives in woodland, so it is described by its habitat.

clue.text: A few deliveries arrived, crushed

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled by one bowler
came means arrived

explanation.surface: Some parcels turned up flattened.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six deliveries (balls bowled); 'deliveries' looks like parcels.
explanation.definitionFit: To crush an opponent is to defeat or beat them, so the past tense matches.

clue.text: Some cop, corrupt, is set up

indicators.note: corrupt says these letters are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: A bent policeman has been framed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' looks like framed but is the printer's sense of arranging type.
explanation.definitionFit: Typesetters arrange type into pages, the old printing sense of setting text.

clue.text: Copy, to appreciate, resembling our close relatives?

parts.note: to ape is to imitate or copy
to like something is to appreciate it

explanation.surface: Imitating and admiring our near kin, we turn out much like them.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'our close relatives' as the great apes, not family members.
explanation.definitionFit: Humans' nearest evolutionary kin are chimps and gorillas, so looking like them is simian.

clue.text: Greek feature partially fills up my loft when returned

indicators.note: returned means the hidden letters are read backwards
partially says only part of the run of words is used, letters spanning them

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs a loft with Greek bric-a-brac brought back from holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partially' picks SUPMYLO from 'fills up my loft'; 'when returned' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest mountain in Greece, a landscape landmark, home of the gods in myth.

clue.text: Run past, wild and free?

indicators.note: wild says these letters run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: A horse bolts past, untamed and at liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: To unbuckle a fastening band is to release or let loose what it held.

clue.text: Society concerned with G & S arias?

parts.note: on means about or concerned with, as in 'a book on birds'
the initials G and S, as written

explanation.surface: An operatic society devoted to Gilbert and Sullivan and their solos.
explanation.walkthrough: G & S is Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic-opera partnership, here just two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Arias are solo pieces in opera, an example of vocal pieces; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Object when nothing put in glass of beer?

indicators.note: put in says the zero is placed inside the drink

parts.note: a pint is the standard glass of beer in a British pub
O resembles zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being served an empty beer glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb (protest) but is the noun meaning aim.
explanation.definitionFit: The object of an exercise is its purpose, as in 'what's the use?'

clue.text: Be punished, with mistake in record of earnings

parts.note: to pay for something is to suffer or be punished for it
a slip is a small mistake

explanation.surface: An employee pays dearly for an error in the wages accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: The note an employer hands over showing wages and deductions for a pay period.

clue.text: Portion of salary earned for a time

indicators.note: Portion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A slice of one's wages is earned over a period of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve months is a period of time; the clue's 'for a time' points at a unit of time.

clue.text: One — a halfwit — regularly seen in services canteen

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter is taken from the following words

explanation.surface: A dimwit is a familiar figure in the military mess hall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of 'One a halfwit'. The NAAFI (Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes) runs shops and canteens for British forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The organisation behind British forces' shops and cafés, so its name stands for the canteen itself.

clue.text: Muriel, maybe, with advert for engine part

parts.note: Muriel Spark was a Scottish novelist, author of The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie
a plug is a piece of promotion or publicity

explanation.surface: A woman named Muriel appears alongside a commercial for a motor component.
explanation.definitionFit: The device in a petrol motor that ignites the fuel mixture with an electric arc.

clue.text: Trace small American coin

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a cent is a US coin, a hundredth of a dollar

explanation.surface: Someone tracks down a tiny US coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A faint smell or hint left behind, as a hound follows a trail.
